title: Exploring how digital services can prevent gambling harms

content.content: Our multidisciplinary team from the Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) has recently completed a discovery into how digital services can help prevent gambling harms. We are now preparing to test ideas that help people understand their situation, decide what to do next and find the support they need.
Why we are doing this

When we talk about ‘gambling harms’, we mean the various negative impacts gambling can have on people who gamble, those close to them, and wider society. These can include impacts on finances, relationships, health, work and other areas of people’s lives.

In March 2026 the charity GambleAware closed. This charity had been funded voluntarily by the Gambling industry and was responsible for prevention and treatment of the harm some people experience from gambling.

The law has since changed, and gambling companies must now pay a statutory levy. This levy is collected by the Gambling Commission on behalf of the Department of Digital, Culture, Media and Sport to fund prevention and treatment of gambling harm.

Under this levy, the Office for Health Improvement and Disparities, part of DHSC, has been commissioned to lead on gambling harms prevention in England. We are also working with prevention commissioners in Scotland and Wales as we develop our digital approach.
What work has happened so far

In October, a small team of DHSC digital specialists completed a discovery phase looking at how digital can help prevent gambling harms, and to plan how we will replace assets we inherited when GambleAware closed.
We worked closely with third sector organisations and two lived experience experts, as well as completing user research with people who gamble and with lived experience of gambling harm.

We know that people need clear and trustworthy information that helps them recognise potential harm and decide what to do. Some people will also need specialist support, such as strategies, tools or treatment services, so we will explore ways to link them to these.

title: Share your evidence on the impacts of recreational activities in England's marine protected areas (MPAs)

content.content: Are you a marine researcher? Do you study seagrass recovery, monitor seal colonies or capture data on marine birds? Are you a passionate diver, wild swimmer, coastal tour operator or experienced sailor? We want to hear from you.

On 30 September 2026, we launched a Call for Evidence on how marine Non-Licensable Activities (mNLAs), including things like anchoring, watercraft, diving and wildlife watching, impact protected habitats and species in England's MPAs.

We've already conducted a substantial literature review examining the current evidence base and pulled this into what we call ‘Impacts Evidence’ documents. We want your views and any additional evidence. This will help us to ensure that fair, evidence led decisions are made about how these areas are managed in the future.
What are mNLAs
They cover a broad range of recreational and commercial activity in and around our coasts, including:
This excludes all fishing activities.

Our draft Impact Evidence documents examine how these activities may impact protected habitats and species, from benthic (seabed) habitats to birds, seals and otters, reef features, seagrass beds, maerl beds, seahorses and stalked jellyfish.
Why we need your evidence

Our draft Impact Evidence documents are a starting point, but in several areas, we believe there is more information available which could help to improve our understanding. Because of this, we're asking anyone with evidence to share it with us now, leading to better-informed, more proportionate decisions later.
If your work touches any of these following areas, your evidence could make a real difference:

Recreational disturbance of wildlife: there is substantial uncertainty around how birds, seals and otters respond to recreational activity including disturbance thresholds, the distances at which activities trigger a reaction, cumulative effects of repeated disturbance, and the long-term consequences for breeding success and survival.

Recovery and resilience of habitats: we need more on how habitats, especially seagrass beds, maerl beds, reefs and benthic sediments, recover from disturbance, how resilient they are to repeated activity, and where the thresholds lie beyond which recovery becomes difficult.

Activity-specific impacts: there's a lack of direct evidence on things like recreational anchoring impacts, hovercraft effects on seals and otters, propeller wash and vessel wake on reefs, and diving and snorkelling impacts on sensitive features. Right now, many assessments rely on evidence from analogous situations rather than direct studies, so direct evidence here is especially valuable.
Spatial and cumulative effects: we want to better understand where activities happen, how often, and how they overlap with protected features.
What evidence are we looking for
We welcome a wide range of evidence and insights that can improve our understanding of the effects of activities on marine protected habitats and species, including:
Scientific and technical evidence, such as research papers, technical reports, monitoring studies, habitat condition assessments, species surveys, theses and conference proceedings.
Site-specific evidence, including local monitoring programmes, citizen science data, visitor-use studies, site management reports, and before-and-after evaluations of management measures.

Operational and practitioner knowledge from harbour authorities, conservation organisations, recreational user groups and others with direct experience of marine environments, including observations of what management approaches have, or have not, worked in practice.

Activity and distribution data, such as vessel activity data, GPS or app-based tracking information, seasonal activity patterns, and spatial data showing where activities overlap with protected habitats or species.
Evidence is particularly valuable when it:

Grey literature, monitoring reports, practitioner knowledge and local observations can all make important contributions. Equally, evidence showing little or no impact is just as valuable as evidence of adverse effects, helping to reduce uncertainty and build confidence in future assessments and management decisions.
What makes evidence particularly useful
Your submission is likely to carry more weight if it:
And don't hold back if your findings show little or no impact, that's just as valuable for building confidence in future assessments.
What happens to the evidence

The evidence you submit will help us build a stronger and more consistent understanding of how activities interact with marine protected habitats and species. We combine evidence from MPAs in England with relevant studies, monitoring data and practical experience from elsewhere in the UK and beyond to develop a robust evidence base for our assessments.

This wider evidence base is used alongside site-specific information to support assessments of impacts and risks within individual MPAs. By contributing evidence, you can help fill important knowledge gaps, improve confidence in our assessments, and inform future decisions about the management and protection of these sites.
Have your say
Whether you're a university researcher, a harbour authority, a conservation group or a recreational sailing or diving club, you have knowledge that can genuinely improve how we manage England's MPAs.
If you hold evidence that speaks to any of the gaps above, we want to hear from you.
Send in your photography

In addition, we’re asking you to share any images of protected marine habitats and species with us. By taking part you will be helping others to explore these often-hidden features of our coast and support MMOs vital conservation work.
When photographing marine wildlife, you should follow the Marine and Coastal Wildlife Code which contains information on how to avoid marine wildlife disturbance.

title: Designing with Strengths, not Deficits

content.content: In September, we ran a workshop at Service Design in Government (SDinGov) in Edinburgh, Scotland called Designing with Strengths, Not Deficits. It was a practical session exploring how we frame people in public services, and what changes when we look beyond need, risk or failure.

The idea comes from strengths-based practice in social work. The Strengths Perspective was first formally articulated in 1989, building on work with adults with psychiatric disabilities and challenging approaches that focused mainly on people's problems or limitations. At its heart, strengths-based practice asks us to see people as resourceful and capable, even in difficult circumstances. It does not mean ignoring harm, risk, need or safeguarding. Those things still matter, but they should not be the whole story.

This way of thinking feels especially relevant to public services. In the UK and around the world, governments are responding to complex needs and constrained resources. We can already see examples of this thinking in justice.

For instance, HMPPS's existing Building Choices programme supports people to develop skills and work towards future-focused goals, without defining them solely by offence labels. Although separate from our work, it reflects the wider shift we are interested in exploring: how can we recognise people's strengths alongside their needs and build support around their potential?

Building on our our experience in local government, social care and working with people with lived experience, we shared two case studies that showed strengths-based thinking in practice. Both demonstrated how services can build on what people already know, do and value, creating conditions for them to bring their strengths and motivation into a programme.

We then introduced two practical activities. The first explored how language shapes our assumptions about people. The second asked participants to generate ideas using only people's needs, before introducing their strengths and wider context. We wanted people to experience the shift for themselves, rather than just talk about it.
Introducing the Strengths-based Discovery Canvas

As part of the SDinGov workshop we also shared an early prototype of  Strengths-based discovery canvas which we hope to test and refine with more teams. The canvas is designed to help teams pause before jumping into research or solutions. It can be used at the start of discovery to challenge assumptions and build a fuller understanding of the people a service is trying to support.

The first part helps teams map the brief they have inherited, including user needs, language that might be limiting their thinking, and the operational constraints they need to work within. The second part asks teams to look at what is already there. They map people's abilities, existing moments of support, relationships and assets. It also asks an important question of what would a good outcome look like for this person or group?

By bringing needs and strengths together, we hope the canvas will help teams identify better research questions, consider more thoughtful ways of engaging with people and recognise opportunities they might otherwise have missed. One participant said: “I found it thought-provoking. I can see how it encourages teams to challenge deficit thinking and it made me realise how much I focus on deficits myself! Good stuff.”
The language we use matters

One of the strongest reflections from the workshop was about language. The words we use shape how people are seen, how teams respond and what kind of support feels possible. This felt particularly relevant in prisons and probation, where words like "non-engagement", "failure" or "risk" may describe something real but can also narrow the frame. Teams might end up noticing missed requirements before understanding the person's circumstances or motivation.

Many participants at SDinGov were service designers and policy professionals. During the activity on deficit-based language, several said they felt like they had their "content designer hat" on. That felt important. Working closely with content designers can help teams develop better patterns and standards for how services communicate.

However, this is not just content design work. It is something multidisciplinary user-centred design (UCD) teams can bring into discovery and alpha. For example, in discovery, instead of only asking “Why are people missing appointments?”, we might also ask, “What helps people attend?” or “Who do they already turn to for support?” In alpha, rather than only testing whether a new feature is easy to use, we could explore whether it builds on people's existing routines, gives them more confidence and makes it easier to take the next step.

This can lead to more meaningful relationships with people and make engagement feel less tokenistic.Rather than engaging people only to validate a solution, teams can better understand what people already rely on and where a digital service could genuinely add value. It also creates opportunities for users, operational colleagues and digital teams to work more closely together.
Testing and developing the approach

We left the session feeling that there is a real appetite for this way of working. Participants were interested in how the canvas could help teams move from a deficit-led brief to a fuller understanding of people and their context.

A strengths-based approach has clear parallels with user-centred design because both depend on meaningful engagement with people. What we do not know yet is where the canvas will bring the most benefit, or how it needs to change to work across different contexts.

That is where we would love input from the wider community. You might work in research, service design, content design, policy, operations or delivery. Whether you are working individually or as part of a team, we would love you to try the canvas and share what works, what feels unclear and what could be improved.
We are hosting an online collaborative session on 27 November 2026 at 10am to explore these questions together and shape the next version of the canvas.
Join the conversation by signing up on Eventbrite. Your ideas and experiences will help us develop an approach that works in practice.

title: Have your say: A closer look at Norfolk’s Environmental Delivery Plan

content.content: By Brad Tooze, Director, Nature Restoration Fund

The Nature Restoration Fund provides a new way to support development while delivering larger-scale improvement for nature. It focusses on achieving an overall benefit for nature, rather than maintaining the status quo.

The first Environmental Delivery Plan (EDP) in England will focus on the impact of nitrogen and phosphorous, otherwise known as nutrient pollution, and has been developed to protect and enhance the Norfolk Broads and River Wensum Special Areas of Conservation and Broadland Ramsar. Following work with local stakeholders, Norfolk’s draft plan is currently going through public consultation, giving you the opportunity to help shape the final approach.
The wider context

The Norfolk Broads and River Wensum have been affected by nutrient pollution for many years, with pollution coming from a range of sources. New development alone did not create these historic problems, and its contribution is relatively small compared with the wider pressures on the water environment.
These wider water quality issues are being addressed through other government and industry action, with significant investments, and the government has announced a commitment to a Water Bill.
What will the EDP do?

The EDP will leave the habitats and species impacted by new development in a better position than they would be in a world than where the EDP (and its associated development and conservation measures) did not exist.

Under the nutrient neutrality system, developments affecting protected sites have to demonstrate that they will not increase nutrient pollution. This is usually achieved by purchasing nutrient credits, which offsets the additional pollution generated by development.

We have proposed a series of measures which will work in combination to deliver real benefits for the identified habitats and species. This includes removing nutrients created by development whilst also supporting wider, lasting improvements to habitat extent, connectivity and quality.

An example of how we have sought to deliver multiple benefits is removing nutrient inputs on land at the same time as improving its environmental quality by changing land use from intensive forms of agriculture to semi-natural habitats. These can also be positioned next to existing and new high-quality areas (including fen creation), improving environmental resilience. Because of the range and scale of pressures on the habitats and species, we need to put in place a package of measures that will both remove nutrients and deliver wider benefits to result in a material improvement which is the key legal test.
The science and evidence behind conservation measures

Natural England undertook an evidence review to investigate the effectiveness of the conservation measures considered for inclusion in the EDP. This review gathered information on environmental benefits, as well as requirements for the measure to be effective (e.g.  location or long-term maintenance needs), time to effectiveness, and potential environmental risks.

Conservation measures were shortlisted by assessing each potential measure against a set of criteria including those relating to delivery, the strength of evidence for their effectiveness, and their potential to deliver a range of environmental benefits suitable for the local area. The approach taken to assess the strength of evidence was recommended in a policy brief produced by researchers at Oxford University (Stuart et al. 2026)).
The approach to conservation measure selection in the EDP was also scrutinised by Defra scientists and external members of Defra’s Biodiversity Expert Committee.
How the Overall Improvement Test works, including the safeguards built into the NRF
This is not a one-off test, but an ongoing commitment by Natural England over at least the lifetime of the EDP, keeping nature at the forefront.
Monitoring and reporting will track delivery, backed by remedial action, back-up measures and powers to amend or revoke an EDP if it is not delivering as expected.
Don’t miss your chance to shape the final EDP
This is a new approach under new legislation, and your feedback matters.
Responses through this consultation will directly inform the final design and approaches helping to ensure the Nature Restoration Fund is practical, proportionate and effective.

A Business Readiness Forum was held on 21 September to walk-through the draft EDP and host an extended Q&A session. You can watch this back on our YouTube channel, and we have a write-up of all questions raised during the Q&A.

title: Standardising construction product data to improve building safety
authors: Buildings, Design and Construction (BDC) digital team

content.content: The Buildings, Design and Construction (BDC) digital team in the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) has been working closely with policy colleagues and stakeholders to explore ways to improve construction safety as part of supporting the recommendations on systemic reforms set out in the Construction Products Reform White Paper.

In this blog post, we share how we’re using user research, mapping data flows and exploring common data standards to help make critical building safety information clearer, consistent and accessible, and how you can get involved.
The problem to solve

Information and data about buildings, things like what they are made of and how safe they are, is often unstructured, inconsistent and of poor quality. The construction industry is also behind many other industries in terms of digital adoption, with a lot of important information and documentation still stored on paper. This can have a negative impact on safety, productivity and innovation.

Important safety information about construction products, such as cladding materials, fire doors and steel, may be unavailable to decision makers like building designers or safety assessors, when they need it. The information may contain inaccuracies or be too ambiguous to be useful. This means critical safety decisions risk being made based on incorrect information or delayed while these data gaps are addressed.

Because data is not standardised, information is manually re-entered across computer systems, which takes time and increases the risk of error. Decision makers might also commission their own surveys or data collection if they can’t trust or understand existing data, resulting in duplicated time and effort.

The government is exploring interventions, including common data standards, to improve the quality of information and how it flows across the lifecycle of a building, from material supply and manufacture through to end of life.
Why does this matter?
The Grenfell Tower Tragedy in 2017 led to a devastating loss of life and revealed systemic failures, including a pervasive crisis in the UK’s construction products regulatory system.

The Grenfell Tower Inquiry identified failings in how product information was handled, including how poor-quality, incomplete and sometimes misleading product information contributed to unsafe decisions about construction products.

In the Construction Products Reform White Paper, the government has committed to wide-reaching systemic reforms. These include creating a single regulator for construction products and making information about construction products clearer and more accessible.
The long-term aim of this work is for information about buildings and construction products to be consistent, easily understood and accessible by everyone who needs it, when they need it.
What we’re doing

Our multidisciplinary discovery team started by agreeing the scope of the work. The project is covering a huge system with potential for further expansion, so this was a critical step. This involved reviewing the existing evidence so we could identify the gaps, agree research questions, and identify key stakeholders to help us with the work.

The team has been mapping the entire building lifecycle to identify and visualise where information is created, maintained, and exchanged between different systems or organisations. To help bring this to life, we mapped the journey of a fire door across the building lifecycle. This takes us all the way from sourcing materials, through testing, supply, building design and installation, maintenance, right through to the end of a building’s life. These systems maps will help us identify where information challenges are most acute and why.

The team has also been researching existing technical data standards. Numerous industry standards exist, but none are consistently adopted. As we think about the future of this work and how to standardise information across the sector, it's important that we understand what we can learn from existing standards and standardisation initiatives and how these help data users across the system.

We’re now diving into some user research, too. This is a critical part of making sure our understanding of the information and data challenges across the system is robust and informed by those actually experiencing the challenges day to day.

To do this, we’re holding targeted stakeholder workshops to strengthen the evidence we have for how construction product data is created, managed, controlled and exchanged. It will also show us where across the building lifecycle users are experiencing the biggest data challenges, and what we can learn from existing standards and initiatives to improve further.
Making the policy process digital
We’ve been working closely with the Digital Front Door team and the wider Construction Products Division to bring policy and digital together to solve these challenges.
This approach has enabled our policy team to:

The BDC digital team is also learning from MHCLG’s Digital Planning team who established the powers to set data standards for local plans in the Levelling Up and Regeneration Act 2023 and Planning Data Regulations 2026.
Get involved – join our show and tells
We want to bring the sector with us on this journey. That’s why we’re hosting open show and tells, which will be used to share our mapping work and emerging insights, and to gather feedback.

The show and tells are open to any interested sector stakeholders and will take place every other Thursday from 11am to 12pm, with the next session scheduled for 5 November. If you’d like to come along, please complete this show and tell registration form.
You can watch our last show and tell held earlier in October.

title: Supporting Digital Mental Health Technology Developers: a new Community of Practice and survey to support regulatory compliance

content.content: In the first of a series of new blog posts focused on compliance issues for medical devices, our Market Surveillance team describes how we will support digital mental health technology developers to understand and navigate the regulatory framework.
Background

The use of software and AI technologies within healthcare is growing rapidly, with many of these technologies playing an increasingly important role in clinical practice and as direct-to-consumer health resources accessible outside of traditional healthcare settings. Depending on their intended purpose and functionality, many of these technologies are regulated as medical devices and are subject to regulatory frameworks intended to ensure safety, effectiveness, and quality.

As with many fast-moving and innovative areas, navigating the regulatory landscape for these technologies can sometimes be complex. Developers may be working across emerging product types, and evolving evidence.

The National Commission into the Regulation of AI in Healthcare has undertaken work to consider the current regulations and make recommendations for a new regulatory framework for AI in healthcare. On 10 September 2026, the National AI Commission published their report Recommendations for a future regulatory framework. The Commission’s central conclusion is that the regulation and assurance of AI in healthcare must become more proportionate, lifecycle-based and system-wide.

The Government published its response on 6 October 2026, accepting all 44 of the recommendations and setting out how they will be taken forward. While this work is taken forward, developers must continue to meet the requirements of the existing regulatory framework.

The National Commission recognised that, as software and AI-enabled medical devices evolve throughout their lifecycle, regulatory oversight needs to evolve with them. It recommended that the MHRA develop more responsive approaches to engagement and compliance, helping manufacturers understand and meet their regulatory responsibilities while enabling issues to be identified and addressed earlier. Accepting this recommendation, we have committed to work with stakeholders to test how these approaches can work in practice, building on work the MHRA was already taking forward to support earlier engagement, strengthen regulatory understanding and address non-compliance.

We recognise the particular regulatory challenges within the Digital Mental Health Technologies (DMHT) landscape, where products often operate across the boundaries of wellbeing and regulated medical device functionality. As a result, this can create challenges for developers on topics such as intended purpose, risk classification (particularly for borderline determinations) and clinical evidence expectations. In addition, the continuous refinement and evolution of these products both during development and after initial market placement means that topics such as usability and post-market monitoring remain especially important activities.

As the sector develops over time, there is a valuable opportunity to develop regulatory approaches and stakeholder engagement strategies that are accessible, agile and capable of supporting innovation while maintaining patient safety and public trust.

We recognise that creating more opportunities for shared discussion and practical engagement can clarify understanding across the sector, improve confidence in navigating these frameworks and support safe and effective innovation whilst embedding regulatory compliance into routine practice across the DMHT landscape. We therefore introducing support for earlier engagement with developers and to encourage practical, sector-wide dialogue that helps teams navigate regulation alongside innovation.
Facilitating a Collaborative Forum within the DMHT Space

To support early engagement and facilitate structured dialogue between the MHRA and the DMHT landscape, we are launching a Community of Practice for developers and manufacturers of DMHTs. The initiative is intended to support capability-building across the sector by creating a collaborative forum focused on developing regulatory understanding throughout the product life cycle.

This Community of Practice will not provide product-specific regulatory advice or endorsement of individual technologies or manufacturers. Instead, it aims to encourage open discussion on common regulatory themes and areas of interest relevant to those within the DMHT sector.

The programme will consist of in-person sessions led by the MHRA and facilitated by an independent host. Utilising feedback received from developers, initial sessions are expected to focus on key areas that frequently pose challenges for developers, including:

A central aim of this work is to better understand which topics developers and manufacturers would find most valuable to explore through a Community of Practice, and where further shared discussion could be most helpful. To support this, we are also launching an anonymous survey for DMHT developers and manufacturers to help shape future sessions. Insights gathered from the survey will help identify common trends and knowledge gaps so that we may prioritise topics for future sessions. Findings will be reviewed across the wider sector to ensure anonymity while informing shared priorities for learning and development. We are planning for the inaugural Community of Practice session to take place in 2027.
Help shape the DMHT Community of Practice: Take part in the survey

The deadline for completing the survey is 11:59pm (UK time) on Thursday 19 November 2026. If you are interested in completing the survey, you may do so via the link below. We will collect data anonymously on your views of your understanding of the following topics, on an assessment scale ranging from ‘Strongly Disagree’ to Strongly Agree’:

The survey is open to all DMHT developers and manufacturers. Completion of the survey does not automatically enrol you in the Community of Practice, as survey responses will be collected anonymously. If you would like to receive information about events and opportunities to get involved, you will have the option to opt in separately and provide your contact details.

This initiative forms part of MHRA’s broader approach to compliance, supporting our new Strategy to 2030, in providing earlier engagement and clearer regulatory guidance, helping innovators and manufacturers navigate regulatory requirements and bring safe, effective products to patients more quickly.

title: The draft Code of Practice for the information gateway has been laid in Parliament

content.content: Today the draft Code of Practice for Public Authorities Sharing Information with Digital Verification Services has been laid in Parliament. This represents a significant milestone in our plans to commence the information gateway.
The Code of Practice

The Code provides guidance which public authorities must have regard to when sharing information with registered digital verification services (DVS) under section 45 of the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025. This power is referred to as the 'information gateway'.

As explained in our previous blog post on the information gateway, the power allows public authorities to share information with registered DVS, as long as certain conditions are met. This includes both direct issuance of government-issued credentials to be stored in registered private sector wallets, and sharing specific attributes or status checks, depending on what's needed for the use case in question. We encourage DVS and public authorities to discuss these requirements as part of establishing data sharing agreements governing use of the power.
Commencement of section 45 (the information gateway)

The Code must now be approved by both Houses of Parliament before it is published as final, which we are aiming to do by the end of the year. Subject to this approval, we also intend to commence section 45 of the Data Act at the same time as the Code is published.

With regards to HMRC, the Welsh Revenue Authority and Revenue Scotland, we will not be commencing section 45 for those three authorities this year. We are continuing to work towards commencing the information gateway for them (and the accompanying provisions in sections 46, 47, and 48), and will set out a timeline for this in due course.
Next steps

We will provide further updates and guidance on the Code and the information gateway on the blog in the coming weeks. This will include confirmation if and when the Code has been approved by Parliament, and commencement of section 45.

title: One simple change and a trust earns over £100,000 a year in extra interest
authors: Judith Haste, Chief Financial Officer at St Edmundsbury and Ipswich Diocesan Multi Academy Trust

content.content: Judith Haste, Chief Financial Officer at St Edmundsbury and Ipswich Diocesan Multi Academy Trust, made up of 21 primary schools in Suffolk, explains how switching to a deposit savings platform has more than doubled its interest-generated income - bringing in more than £100,000 a year that goes straight back into supporting children's education.
Our money was sitting still and losing out
Our money was sitting in a standard current account earning very little interest. I knew the rates were not competitive and we could do much better.

I’d got experience of using a savings platform from a previous trust, and in particular the Department for Education (DfE) approved Insignis platform. The service lets you move funds into higher-interest accounts quickly and easily all in one place, without opening separate accounts with different providers.

Before platforms like this existed, moving money around was a real headache. You needed board approvals for every account you wanted to open. It was slow and impractical. These platforms changed all of that.

I chose the Insignis platform again because it offered clear, transparent pricing. That mattered to me. When you are working with public money, you need to know exactly what you are paying and what you are getting back.
What we actually do each month
At the start of each month, our General Annual Grant (GAG) funding arrives. I look at what we need to keep back for payroll, HMRC payments, and any other known costs.

Then I look at where to place other funds based on the frequency of access, and where we will get the best return. For example, I will place some into an instant access account, some goes into a 30-day notice account for a better rate, and some we fix for a full year, because we don’t expect to need access in the near future.
We think of it as layering our funds. Each layer earns a better rate the longer it can be left. It takes a small amount of time at the start and end of each month and that’s it.
We also set up something called sweeping on our current account. Every day, any surplus automatically moves into our instant access account. If we need the money back, it pulls the other way.
Nobody has to do anything, it’s automated and means we are always earning interest on ‘idle’ cash with little impact on our time.
What this has meant in real terms for our trust
The numbers speak for themselves. We now earn around £4,500 to £5,000 a month from the returns, plus another £1,000 to £2,000 a month from our instant access sweeping.

Before, we were earning around £1,000 to £2,000 a month in total. We have more than doubled our interest income. St Edmundsbury and Ipswich Diocesan MAT now brings in over £100,000 a year in extra interest. This is a significant sum that could fund additional staff, resources or support directly for pupils.
The platform isn't free, but the returns we've achieved make the fee negligible by comparison, and the financial benefit to the school speaks for itself.

I understand why some people feel nervous; treasury management can sound complicated. But you can manage the risk sensibly and spreading funds across providers actually reduces risk compared to leaving everything in one account.
It works for schools and trust of all sizes

Our trust wrote a clear investment policy. It sets out the credit ratings we require and confirms that all deposits must be United Kingdom-based. This gives our trustees the confidence they need and gives me a clear framework to work within.
You do not have to be a large trust or school to benefit and the interest earned can run into tens of thousands of pounds a year.
It is worth exploring the platform, it’s easy and straightforward to use. Onboarding is simple and the Insignis helpdesk is there when you need it. And once you are set up, it really does run itself.
My honest advice to other school business professionals - this is not complicated. Make sure you have a good investment policy, trustee support, and the willingness to take that first step.

If I had one tip for anyone not yet doing this, it would be this: start with sweeping. It is the easiest win available. Set it up once and it works for you every single day, without any effort at all.

title: Part 1: What Are Marine Protected Areas, and Why Do They Matter?

content.content: As the Convention on Biological Diversity COP17 begins in Yerevan, Armenia, this week, the global 30 by 30 target will be firmly in focus: conserving and effectively managing at least 30% of the world’s land, inland waters, coastal areas and ocean by 2030. Marine Protected Areas are central to achieving that ambition—but their success depends on more than designation. Through the UK Government’s Blue Belt Programme, the UK Overseas Territories receive scientific, technical and management support to protect over 4 million square kilometres ocean. This three-part series explores what that looks like in practice, from MPA design and management to long-term monitoring and adaptation.
So, you want to protect an area of the ocean and all that lives within it. How do you go about doing this?
Maybe you'd consider establishing a Marine Protected Area, or MPA. Close off a not insignificant area of ocean and prohibit all human activity.
Job done, right?
Not quite. MPAs are far more nuanced, and far more interesting, than a line drawn on a map.

When designed well, governed equitably and managed effectively, MPAs are one of the most effective tools we have for marine conservation. They are a cornerstone of efforts to safeguard the unique marine ecosystems of the UK Overseas Territories and support the long-term health and resilience of our oceans.

While definitions vary, an MPA is broadly understood as a clearly defined area of ocean that is designated and managed to achieve the long-term protection of habitats, species or whole ecosystems. By managing human activities and reducing pressures on the marine environment, MPAs help ecosystems recover, rebuild biodiversity and become more resilient to future threats.
Not all MPAs are the same
MPAs exist along a spectrum of protection, depending on what they've been designated to achieve.
At one end, fully or highly protected MPAs, or no-take zones, are explicitly shielded from damaging and extractive human activities such as fishing, mining, and oil and gas drilling and production.

At the other end are sustainable use MPAs, where conservation and carefully managed human activities coexist. Fishing, tourism and recreation may be permitted under specific regulations, provided they're carried out in a way that maintains or helps improve the health, biodiversity and ecological integrity of the marine environment for future generations.

Many MPAs combine both approaches through zoning, allowing different levels of protection to work together as part of a wider marine management framework. Ascension Island offers a striking example. It has the third largest MPA in the South Atlantic, an area of ocean the size of France, stewarded by a tiny island. Around 90% of this MPA is a no-take zone, but along its coast, recreational and subsistence fishing is allowed by local communities.

Regardless of design or level of protection, all MPAs share the same fundamental purpose: to conserve biodiversity, protect endangered and vulnerable species, preserve critical habitats and maintain healthy, functioning marine ecosystems.
It's not just about the wildlife
The ecological benefits of MPAs are well recognised, but their value extends far beyond protecting habitats and species.

Well-managed MPAs can support healthier fish stocks and improve fisheries productivity through what's known as the "spillover" effect, where fish and other marine species move beyond protected boundaries into surrounding waters. This can help replenish depleted stocks, improve catches, strengthen food security and increase household incomes in coastal communities. The benefits often extend through the wider seafood supply chain too, supporting fishers, processors and exporters. At the same time, MPAs can create new opportunities for marine nature-based tourism such as snorkelling and wildlife watching, generating jobs, diversifying local economies and reducing reliance on a single source of income.

MPAs also provide important social and cultural benefits. When designed and managed with local communities, they can foster a great sense of pride, environmental stewardship and connection to the marine environment, while preserving cultural traditions and creating opportunities for recreation and improved wellbeing.

Increasingly, MPAs are recognised as valuable tools for climate change mitigation and adaptation. By protecting blue carbon habitats such as mangroves, seagrass and kelp, MPAs help store carbon and reduce emissions from habitat degradation. Healthy coastal ecosystems also act as natural defences against storms, flooding and erosion, helping communities adapt to a changing climate.

From supporting sustainable fisheries and tourism to strengthening climate resilience, MPAs provide a wide range of benefits for both people and nature. In our next blog, we'll look at how MPAs are actually managed, because designating one is just the beginning of the story.

title: Improving support for people who need help using online court and tribunal services
authors: Miriam Davidson - Head of User Inclusion and Engagement, HMCTS

content.content: [English] - [Cymraeg]

More court and tribunal services are available online than ever before. For many people, this makes it easier to access justice. But we know that not everyone has the technology, skills or confidence needed to use digital services.

That's why we offer the Digital Support Service. The service helps people who do not have access, whether through a lack of internet access or device, skills or confidence - to benefit from our online services.
From April 2027, we're changing how support is delivered, and I want to share with you how this will improve the experience of some of our most disadvantaged users.
Understanding the barriers people face

Digital exclusion is often linked to other challenges people may be experiencing. Someone may be living with a disability or health condition, struggling financially, facing language barriers, or dealing with a stressful and difficult situation. People living in rural areas can also face challenges, such as poor internet connectivity or limited access to digital services.

Greater understanding about our users needs means our approach cannot follow a one-size-fits-all solution. In the future, support will be able to identify wider needs, adapt the way help is provided, and, where appropriate, connect someone with other sources of support beyond their immediate digital problem.
A more local approach to support
To define our future service, we used evidence from the current service, an independent evaluation and extensive engagement with organisations that support digitally excluded people.

What we heard was clear. Local organisations often have a better understanding of the communities they serve and can reach people who may not know support is available.  From April 2027, Digital Support will be delivered through 11 regional grants covering England, Wales and Scotland, rather than through a single national provider.

The successful organisations are all part of the Citizens Advice network. Each organisation will run support in their region, working in partnership with other Citizens Advice organisations to make sure support is available across their region.

They also plan to work in trusted community settings including libraries, community centres and health settings, enabling us to reach our users where they are based, rather than forcing them to visit a potentially unfamiliar building. The organisations awarded funding are listed at the end of this blog.

Because our new partners are familiar with our work, support will cover all our online services and new ones as they're introduced, this is important because it means people can be helped immediately to access new services and without needing to wait for our partners to update their systems or train their staff.
What this means for users

For those experiencing digital exclusion, often alongside other complex and overlapping barriers, the changes will make sure help reaches the people who need it most, so that everyone can access justice.

Courts and tribunals users will continue to receive tailored support, whether that's help completing forms, accessing clear guidance, or more intensive one-to-one support to understand a process or upload evidence. It will be available face-to-face, by telephone or remotely, and people will be able to ask for help directly or access assistance through a direct referral from HMCTS.

This means that whether a person is responding to a Single Justice Notice, appealing a benefit decision or applying for help with fees, they can benefit from support to complete an online court form and access justice.

title: Test, Learn and Grow, one year on
authors: Nick Kimber – Director for Public Service Reform, Cabinet Office

content.content: Two years ago, I sat in a room with a small team to explore whether starting small, testing assumptions against real-world evidence, and bringing policy and delivery together in the same room could help build better public services, faster.
What if local government and communities worked with central government in a radically different way, putting partnership at the centre?

One year ago, we started putting those thoughts into practice with local authority partners across ten places. A lot has changed. The programme has become a community of change makers, a network of almost 2000 members, convenors from across the public sector lending their credibility and time, and a growing body of evidence about what actually happens when you try to change how government works from the inside out.

The recent publication of Rewiring the State set out a clear and ambitious context for exactly this kind of place-based reform. This means the Test, Learn and Grow (TLG) programme is no longer just making the case for a different way of working; the case has, in large part, already been made elsewhere, and more loudly than we could have made it ourselves.
What's exciting now is that we get to move into the hard yards: delivering the reform, and nurturing the mindsets, practices and organisational capabilities that make it stick.
What we set out to do, and what actually happened

At the time of starting the programme in 2024, we believed we could prove our initial question was true regardless of whether a technology or data solution was involved, and we wanted to show that the practices pioneered in digital service design could become a mainstream way of developing policy, not a niche one.

Mostly, that hypothesis has held up. But it's also been harder than any of us expected. There have been times where we found that an idea we were confident about simply didn't survive contact with the people it was meant to serve. None of that is failure in the way failure is usually talked about in government. We only know how an assumption plays out when we test it, not when we imagine it. Starting small means these setbacks are cheap, and they teach us something we couldn't have learned any other way. Failure is what happens when you commit large amounts of resource and attention without de-risking your approach through real world evidence.

What I've found most useful this year is a growing clarity about why TLG works. It isn't one method. It's really the combination of three different traditions. There's relational practice, anchored in communities, that works with the strengths and assets already present in the places we work alongside, rather than treating people as problems to be fixed. There's digital practice, with its internet-era instinct to start with the needs of the individual rather than the structure of the organisation. And there's policy, which sets the agenda and brings evidence in order to create the frameworks for legislation and investment that set the conditions for delivery. TLG doesn't ask teams to choose between these. It asks them to be curious about which combination fits the problem in front of them, with learning and adaptation as the thread that runs through all of them.
What we've learned as a movement

The thing I didn't fully anticipate a year ago was how much of this would end up being about people finding each other. Our humble LinkedIn network has rapidly grown to almost 2000 members, comprising council officials, civil servants, voluntary sector and wider public sector partners showing the thirst for people to be part of this work.

We've run an Unconference that brought together more than a hundred people who, in many cases, had been working in isolation on strikingly similar problems. The Department for Education has launched a sister team - a very first dedicated unit set up to take on the TLG approach, working alongside the Cabinet Office and sharing learnings. The test-and-learn network in the South West has formed and there’s genuine buzz and demand for this approach to public service reform, well beyond the ten TLG places themselves. We have welcomed four brilliant TLG convenors, Catherine Howe (Chief Executive, Dorset Council), Beth Russell (Second Permanent Secretary, HM Treasury), Paul Morrison (Director General, Home Office), and Emma De Closset (Chief Executive, UK Community Foundations) who publicly advocate for the network and sponsor initiatives.

This, alongside the Magenta Book annexe we published earlier this year, is part of building the infrastructure needed to support people working to solve complex problems by starting small, focusing on the needs of the individual, and closing the gap between policy and delivery.

And we’ve captured all of this learning into a shared resource published yesterday: the Test, Learn and Grow playbook, a huge achievement and powerful resource to build on. On 20 October, we marked this with a dedicated celebration event in Sheffield alongside Kate Joseph, Chief Executive of Sheffield City Council and her team.
The harder truths

The work shows real promise but it’s also been really hard. There are things we would do differently and ways we could have gone faster or deeper and I want to be honest about what hasn't gone as smoothly. Data-sharing remains one of the most persistent blockers we face. Progress on some of our Grow work, removing the funding and governance barriers that sit underneath all of this, has been slower than I'd like, partly because changing how money and accountability flow is simply harder and slower than running a small test to show how we could improve a service.

There's a deeper truth underneath both of these. We think that for any approach to genuinely count as Test, Learn and Grow, it has to be deeply curious about the conditions needed to learn, adapt and improve, whether that's inside a local authority, an NHS trust, or a central government department. Many of those conditions are set by the centre, even where there's room to interpret the rules differently. That's why we call this work Grow: it's how we grow the conditions for organisations to solve problems alongside the people they serve, rather than in spite of the system around them. It's slower and less visible than the test-and-learn work in our accelerators, but essential to make the important shifts we need for this work to be easier than it is today.

Creating the right conditions means working bottom up, trusting the agility and creativity of people closest to those we serve, and top down, with leaders willing to hold space and risk for people with less power than themselves. We need both.
The Test, Learn & Grow Playbook
The publication of our Test, Learn and Grow playbook yesterday is an important milestone and reflects the progress we’ve made so far, as well as how far we have left to go.

The playbook turns a year of frontline experience into a practical and accessible guide, written by the people who have actually done this work, for others who want to do the same. It was built through real work and experiences in places, not written in advance of it. It will be updated more than once over the life of the programme, and we hope beyond it, as we learn more, and we expect that process to become more inclusive and democratic as the community around TLG grows.

It responds to a genuine demand from central and local government for resources to support the application of test and learn, from the practitioner who is ambitious for change and needs practical, honest support to make it happen, to the leader who has the power to make this way of working possible or stop it in its tracks. The approach we’ve taken has been to do the work, learn as we go, and share so others can respond.  This playbook is one of the main ways we intend to do that.

It’s not prescriptive. We don't think any one organisation will have all the resources it needs to work this way all of the time, even if it wanted to, so the test for us isn't only what works, but what's useful to the widest possible number of people. At its best, we'd like to see a place or an organisation take what we've put together and build their own version of it, under their own steam, adding to a shared pool of knowledge rather than waiting for permission from the centre. This is an invitation to be part of this movement, not an announcement that the work is done.
Looking ahead

None of this is a victory lap. If anything, the better we get at this, the more clearly we can see how much further there is to go. In year two, our focus will be on removing and challenging the foundational barriers that make this work hard to implement and deepening our partnership with local government so that this work increasingly sits with places themselves rather than depending on a central team.

Rewiring the State may have changed the context we're working in but our job now is the harder one of delivering it, and building the mindsets and capabilities that make it last. The real test is whether this work helps services become integrated, preventative, relational and genuinely curious, continuously improving as they go, rather than treating that as a one-off project.

The clearest lesson from a year on from the launch of our accelerator projects is the power of combining traditions rather than choosing between them: relational practice that builds on local strengths, digital practice that starts from individual need, and policy practice that sets the strategic framework. Put together, with learning running through all three, they're more powerful than any one alone.

title: Coverage of Private Parking Code of Practice

content.content: Today we laid the new Private Parking Code of Practice before Parliament. This landmark reform will give drivers new rights to challenge unfair private parking charges.

There has been widespread coverage across national media. This includes articles in The Sun, The Guardian, BBC News Online, the Standard, i News, The Times, The Independent, The Telegraph and the Daily Star, which all covered the new Code's guarantee of 5 minutes for drivers to decide whether to park and 10 minutes to leave once a session ends. Outlets also covered the plans to scrap charges on appeal for situations outside a driver’s control like vehicle breakdowns and medical emergencies,  and the £20 cap on appeal for small slip ups like forgetting a permit or typing in the wrong vehicle registration. Several outlets note this follows a record 16.9 million parking tickets issued last year.

On the morning round, Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government, Angela Rayner was asked about the announcement and spoke about the benefits of the Code to Times Radio, Sky News Breakfast, BBC Breakfast, LBC, BBC Radio 4’s Today, Good Morning Britain, ITN and Bauer. Additional broadcast coverage featured on outlets including BBC Manchester, Greatest Hits Liverpool & North West, Hits Radio Teeside.

And there was further coverage seen in Auto Express,  Buckinghamshire Live, Eastern Daily Press, Regit, Highways Magazine, The Herts Advertiser, West Bridgford Wire, Oxford Mail, Manchester Evening News, Liverpool Echo, Scotsman, AOL and Fleet News.
Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government Angela Rayner said:

“Parking should be straightforward, not another everyday hassle. These changes mean drivers get a fairer deal, protected time to park and leave without fear of being unfairly charged, and confidence that private parking providers are held to a higher standard.
“It’s yet another step forward in this government’s plan to take the stress out of everyday life and ease the pressure on people’s pockets.”
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said:
“Being a few minutes late back to your car or typing one digit of your numberplate wrong shouldn’t end with a hefty fine landing on your doormat.
“These charges leave people feeling ripped off and out of pocket, so I’m putting a stop to them.
“We are introducing clearer rules, longer grace periods and lower charges for genuine mistakes, while going after the deliberate scams that rip drivers off.”
